question.text: The height of victoria's falls is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>63</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">m</mi></math>. What is the difference in the temperature of water at the top and at the bottom of the fall? [Given <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cal</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi></math> and specific heat of water <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced open="" close="]"><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cal</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">g</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo> </mo><msup><mmultiscripts><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mprescripts/><none/><mo>∘</mo></mmultiscripts><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced></math>

solution.text: Here use the concept of conservation of energy, here potential energy is converted in to heat energy, ⇒mgh=msΔθ, here m, h & s, is the mass of the liquid, height of the fall, and specific heat capacity then, g×63=Δθ×4.2×103⇒Δθ=0.147°C.
